7.4 — Ladders II: Mounts, Tops & Polish

Your ladder works in the middle and fails at both ends. Climb it and keep holding W: you rise into the ceiling, or hover at the seam, or fall off the moment the zone ends. The middle of a ladder is easy. The last three tiles are the hardest problem in platformer engineering, and nobody has solved them for you — there are no ladders in this project except the one you built in 7.3.

In this lesson you will be able to answer“how do I stop my ladder breaking at the top and bottom?”Outline only
Break It Down~10 minOutline only

A climb that starts when the player means it to and stops when the player has arrived — at the bottom, at the top, and everywhere the trigger zone and the ladder picture disagree about where either of those is.

First, before any code: cut that into parts small enough that you could look each one up on its own.

  1. Say when the climb startswhat does this part do?Read: 7.3 — the trigger zone and the two callbacks it sends
  2. List every way the climb can endwhat does this part do?Read: 7.3 — the climb flag on PlayerController, and every place that reads it
  3. Ask "have I arrived?" with the ground check you already ownwhat does this part do?Read: 6.2 — the ground check you chose: raycast, overlap circle, or touching layers
  4. Re-tune that check for a player who is climbingwhat does this part do?Read: 7.2 — the Ground layer you made, and the mask you repaired to use it
  5. Decide where a climb with nothing to arrive at endswhat does this part do?Read: 7.2 — the Collision tilemap, and the paint-on-the-right-layer decision
  6. Order the arrival check against the climb movementwhat does this part do?Read: the climb branch you wrote into Update in 7.3, on top of the movement from 1.4
  7. Make the mount readable, or decide it does not need to bewhat does this part do?Read: 5.3 — the Canvas HUD, and the one scene that owns it

Every part above can be answered out loud, in one sentence, before the script is open — and that is the whole test. The climb mechanism already exists and does not change; what fails at the ends of a ladder is a handful of independent decisions that all wear the same symptom until they are separated. The reach of the arrival check, the order of two branches inside one Update, and the frame the exit runs on are three different failures with three different fixes, and a student who treats them as one thing called "the ladder is broken" changes all three at once and learns nothing from the result.

The two-minute test: can you answer the part in one sentence without opening Unity? "Where the climb ends when there is no ledge above it" passes. "Fix the top of the ladder" does not — a part that names a symptom instead of a decision is not a part yet, it is the problem again in fewer words.

Your turn

Pick two of the parts above and say in one line what each one actually does.

Two exits can want to fire on the same frame — the cap stops the player and the arrival check agrees there is floor beneath them. Say which one you want to win, and describe what the player sees during the frame it takes to find out.

A capped ladder moves the last step out of your script and into level design. Name one thing that gets easier because of that, and one thing a tester can break that no line of code can protect against.

The bottom of a ladder is the mirror of the top: the zone ends and the player is standing on nothing. Which of your exits covers that case today, and what does the player see if none of them does?

The Problem: The Top of the Ladder ~15 min

Climb your ladder from 7.3 and hold W past the top tile. Write down exactly what happens — every build does something slightly different, and yours is the only build that matters. Then read the three classic answers:

AnswerWhat the player feelsWhat it costs you
Stop at the top. While climbing, ask whether there is floor under your feet; if there is, leave the climb state and stand up. Honest and sudden. The climb ends the moment you have arrived. One more physics question per frame, and a precise definition of "at the top".
Pop off. Holding W past the top applies a small upward hop that carries you onto the ledge. Flows straight into a jump. Can feel generous or magical. Fiddly physics. The hop can overshoot into a spike or an enemy you never saw.
Cap the ladder. Paint a solid tile above the top of the strip so the player simply stops under it, then jumps the last bit. Blunt and completely learnable. Every player reads it instantly. Level design must guarantee the last jump is possible with the jump you tuned in 6.1. Zero new code.
The cheapest answer is a tile, not a script. Option three requires no new code at all — it is one painted tile on the Collision tilemap, and it works because 7.2 already made that tilemap solid. Before you write anything, check whether your level can simply be shaped to solve the problem. A great deal of platformer engineering is avoided by moving one tile.

Socratic: Who Decides Where the Climb Ends?

  1. Which of the three answers does your build currently have — by accident, not by choice? Say what the player sees at the top tile right now.
  2. Option three costs no code and option one costs a per-frame physics question. Which one teaches the player more about your game's rules, and which one is easier to explain to a tester?
  3. If you cap the ladder, the last step is a jump. What must be true about the height between the cap and the ledge above it? Which number from 6.1 — or which pair of numbers — decides it?
Read Function-Level Examples ~10 min

Each of these is a machine that has to know when to stop. Read each one for what it does in isolation, then find the piece that maps onto the top of your ladder.

Example 1 — A lift levelling itself with a landing, in a hoist controller:

// The car stops when its floor lines up with the landing floor,
// not at the end of the shaft.
if (Mathf.Abs(carFloorY - landingY) < tolerance) StopCar();

Example 2 — A crane's limit switch, cutting the motor at the top of the arc:

private bool atLimit;   // set by the switch, cleared when the hook descends

Example 3 — An escalator's comb plate at the top landing:

// The same tread that carried you up lets you walk off level.
// Nothing lifts you - you simply stop being carried.

Example 4 — An aircraft boarding stair's handrail (comment only):

// The rail is only a rail while someone is on the steps. It is
// not a wall, and it never appears in the doorway.

Example 5 — A stage's fly floor and its counterweight (comment only):

// The rope takes the weight, the floor takes it back. The moment
// is a handover, and handovers are where the bugs live.
Architectural specification: ending the climb cleanly.
  • Which question do you ask to detect "I have arrived"? Name the exact API you already own from 6.2 — you built a ground check there, in whatever form you chose. Reuse it; do not write a second one.
  • How far down does that question need to reach while you are climbing? Your normal ground check distance was tuned for walking. What number would miss the ledge, and what does an over-long reach risk detecting instead?
  • What is the very first thing that must happen when you decide the climb is over — the state flag, the gravity, or the movement? Justify the order.
  • Which branch of your Update runs first: the climb movement or the arrival check? If the movement runs first on the frame you arrive, what does the player do for one frame, and does anyone see it?
  • When you leave the climb state at the top, do you snap the player onto the ledge or let physics settle them? Argue both, then choose.
  • How do you know you have not broken the ordinary ground check for walking? Name the test you will run after the change.
The order-of-operations bug will not announce itself. If your climb branch moves the player before you check whether the climb has ended, then on the arrival frame you move once more and then stop — a single frame of drift into the tile above. At 60 frames per second that is a millimetre. At a low frame rate, on a slow machine, it is enough to shove the player inside a collider that then pushes them out sideways. Find the order in your own Update, write it down, and test at a deliberately low frame rate before you decide it does not matter.
Build Lab: Mount, Cap, and What a Climb Would Take ~30 min

Step 1 — solve the top. Choose one of the three answers and build it. You have already read the costs. If you choose the capped ladder, paint the cap tile first and test the last jump before you write a line of code — if the jump does not clear it, the answer is to move the cap, not to add a pop-off.

Step 2 — the mount decision. Walk into a ladder and nothing happens until you press W. That is one design. Another is that stepping into the zone mounts you automatically and you hang there. A third is that the ladder only grabs you if you press W while inside the zone, so walking past it sideways never snags you. Read all three, choose one, and answer the question that decides it: what does the player expect when they walk past a ladder on the ground?

Step 3 — the mount prompt, or its absence. The bottom of a tall ladder can be out of reach or hard to read. Three honest options, and the project supports all of them:

PromptWhat the player seesWhat it costs
Nothing at all — make the ladder obvious through geometry and tiles A ladder that looks climbable Nothing. And it is the option real games choose most often.
A Debug.Log line while the mount is possible The Console, which your player cannot see Nothing. The HUD you built in 5.3 lives in Start and shows your own stats — it is not in this scene and does not know a ladder exists, so anything you want to watch here is still a Console line.
A world-space text object (a TextMesh in the scene) toggled active while the mount is possible Floating text, in the world, above the ladder A new object, a new reference, and a rule about when it disappears.

Whatever you choose, the rule is the same one you applied to the spike and the coin: a prompt dies the instant it is obeyed or no longer relevant. A prompt that lingers after you have started climbing is worse than no prompt.

What adding a real climb animation would actually involve. You may have noticed your character rises up the ladder in a standing pose. That is not an oversight — it is the honest state of the project. The Player's Animator controller contains exactly three motions, Idle, Walk and Shovel_Swing, and each of those exists in Up, Horizontal and Down variants, driven by the IsWalking, WalkDir and Attack parameters you built in Unit 1. There is no climb state, no climb clip, and no climbing pose in any sprite sheet that ships with this project — check Assets/Artwork/Character/Player/ and its ExtraSpriteSheets/ folder if you want to confirm that yourself.

So if you want a climb animation, here is the whole job, in order, and none of it is today's work:
  • Get frames. Either draw climbing poses, or find a licensed sheet. This is the step that stops most students, and it is art, not code.
  • Import and slice the sheet in the Sprite Editor — the same workflow you met in Unit 1 — so each pose is its own sprite.
  • Author two clips, a climb-idle and a climb-move, or one clip for both if you are being economical.
  • Add the states to the controller and wire transitions in and out of them.
  • Add a parameter — a Bool named for climbing — and drive it from the same state flag your trigger zone already writes.
  • Decide the Up/Down question: do you need a mirrored clip, or does one climb pose read correctly in both directions?
If you do decide to take that on later, it belongs to 7.7's polish pass or to Unit 8 — not to a mechanic that already works.

Step 4 — polish passes. Pick two, and no more.

  • Ladder edges: at the very bottom of the climb state, restore a moment of gravity so the player settles onto the floor instead of hanging in the air when the zone ends.
  • Ladders through one-way ledges: if you built a one-way platform in 7.2, a climb can pass up through the cap. The two features love each other — test it and write down what happens.
  • Sound: one soft tick per tile climbed. You are not adding audio today unless you already have a clip; note it as a candidate instead.
  • The re-entry repair from 7.3: if you chose the cooldown, tune its length. Time it with a stopwatch, not by feel.

Checkpoint — before moving on, you must be able to:

  • Explain the top-of-ladder problem and name the three classic answers with a cost for each
  • Say which answer you built, and why it fits your level
  • Reuse your 6.2 ground check to end the climb, and explain why the reach had to change
  • Defend your mount rule and your prompt decision — including choosing no prompt
  • State honestly that this project ships no climb frames, and list what adding one would involve
  • Break this task into parts small enough to look each one up on its own, and say in one line what each part does
  • Say which earlier lesson each part of this task came from, and where you would reread it
  • Commit and push
